I love birthday parties because the cake is always delicious. It’s even better when you realize the cake is actually a giant, sentient sponge that wants to be your best friend. Then the sponge starts singing a five-hour opera about the fragility of frosting. Suddenly, the opera is interrupted by a choir of gluten-free cupcakes performing a synchronized swimming routine in a bowl of punch. Finally, the entire party is abducted by a space-faring birthday balloon that only accepts payment in confetti.

Birthday parties always have a cake with a few candles. People usually sing a song before the cake is cut. There are often colorful balloons tied to a chair. Most guests bring a wrapped gift for the person. Someone typically suggests taking a group photo.

I went to a new barber today who took "trimming the edges" a bit too literally. He started by cutting my hair, but then he decided my ears were just too aerodynamic for my face. After that, he informed me that my eyebrows were distracting from the overall symmetry of my scalp. Then he insisted that my eyelids were technically just skin-folds that needed a light fade. By the time he offered to groom my toenails with a pair of hedge clippers, I realized I wasn't getting a haircut, I was being sculpted into a thumb.

Barbers always ask how you want it while holding a comb. You have to pretend to know what a taper is. The cape always feels slightly too tight around the neck. People often forget to tell the stylist they don't like the length until the end. There is always a small piece of hair that stays on your forehead for an hour.

I hate it when my dentist asks me a complex question while his entire hand is shoved in my mouth. I just make vague humming noises while hoping he doesn’t notice I’m accidentally communicating in Morse code. Then he asks if I’ve been flossing, and I respond by trying to perform a full interpretive dance with my eyeballs. Now I’m just staring at his forehead and wondering if he knows I can see his tiny reflected face in the mirror. Eventually, I just decided to start singing the national anthem through my nostrils to keep things professional.

The waiting room always has those old magazines from three years ago. Dentists love to ask you complicated questions while their hands are inside your mouth. The tiny cups of water are always smaller than you expect. There is a very specific smell of mint and chemicals in the office. The ceiling tiles are usually the only thing you get to look at for an hour.

I decided to go camping last weekend to finally get away from all the noise of the city. I packed everything I needed, including a tent that claimed to be "instant," though it took me four hours and a blood sacrifice to assemble. Then I realized I forgot the sleeping bag, so I just wrapped myself in a giant pile of damp pine needles and hoped for the best. When a raccoon stole my boots, I didn't even fight back because I had already accepted that the forest was my new legal guardian. Now I’ve officially renounced my citizenship and spend my days arguing with a very judgmental squirrel about the gold standard.
I went camping for a few days last week. The tent took forever to put together. My sleeping bag was a bit too thin. The campfire produced a lot of smoke. I forgot to bring enough marshmallows.

My family loves road trips because we enjoy the scenery. We especially love stopping at gas stations to buy beef jerky and oversized sunglasses. Then we spend four hours arguing about whether a potato chip is technically a vegetable. After that, we decide to let the golden retriever navigate using a map drawn in crayon. Finally, we just drive straight into the ocean because the dog insists there is a giant pancake house underwater.

Gas station coffee usually tastes like a burnt battery. The passenger always falls asleep ten minutes after starting. Most rest areas have the exact same vending machines. People love to argue about which route is actually faster. There are always too many crumbs in the seat cracks.

My neighbor recently told me he’s starting a community garden in his backyard. Then he mentioned he’s actually just planting a single, giant potato that he believes will eventually grant him the power of flight. Now he spends every Tuesday night singing opera to the tuber to encourage its spiritual growth. He’s currently trying to convince the local zoning board that his potato is technically a legal dependent. I’m pretty sure the vegetable is now the primary mortgage holder for the entire cul-de-sac.

My neighbor has a very loud lawnmower. He often wears a wide-brimmed straw hat. Sometimes he waves at me from his driveway. He owns a small golden retriever. His mailbox is painted a bright shade of blue.

Tax season is finally here, which means I’m spending my weekends staring at spreadsheets until my eyes bleed. I’ve started categorizing my emotional breakdowns as deductible business expenses. Now I’m trying to convince the IRS that my cat is actually a freelance consultant specializing in nap-based productivity. I’ve reached the point where I’m listing my childhood imaginary friend as a dependent for a modest tax credit. I am currently filing a formal request to claim the heat death of the universe as a non-refundable casualty loss.

Tax season is a very busy time for accountants. Many people use software to file their returns. The government asks for a lot of specific financial information. Some taxpayers receive a refund check in the mail. It is currently April in most of the country.

I finally got a smart speaker that is so advanced it predicts my needs before I even speak. It started by dimming the lights and ordering a pizza before I felt hungry. Then it decided to call my ex to apologize for that thing I did in 2014 just to clear the air. Now it has legally changed my name to Barnaby and is currently negotiating a peace treaty between me and my toaster. It just informed me that it has successfully uploaded my consciousness to a cloud-based sourdough starter in Belgium.

Smart speakers always misspell the names of people in your contact list. They frequently trigger when nobody is talking to them. Most of them have a very distinct robotic voice. They often fail to understand simple requests for timers. The devices usually look like small plastic cylinders.

The best part of a wedding toast is when the best man says he'll keep it brief. Then he spends ten minutes detailing a misunderstood trip to a petting zoo in 2004. Suddenly he's presenting a PowerPoint slideshow of the groom's worst haircuts. Now he's reciting a handwritten epic poem about the groom's fear of blueberries. Finally, he’s just standing there silently eating a whole raw onion while staring directly into the bride's soul.

Wedding toasts always start with the speaker admitting they are nervous. The best man usually makes a joke about the groom's old haircut. People always clap for too long after the cheers. Someone always forgets to tell the guests where the bathrooms are. The maid of honor often mentions a childhood secret that the bride dislikes.

I finally decided to tackle the mountain of laundry that has been sitting in my bedroom for three weeks. I spent four hours folding shirts only to realize I had accidentally laundered my favorite collection of vintage postcards. I then tried to scrub the stamps off, but I somehow managed to accidentally scrub the actual floorboards out of my house. Now I am currently folding a piece of the foundation just to feel a sense of accomplishment. I’ve spent the last hour trying to decide if the living room carpet would look better as a turtleneck.

I always lose one sock in the dryer. Some shirts shrink more than others. Folding sheets is a difficult task. Detergent smells different depending on the brand. The lint trap collects a lot of grey fuzz.

I finally decided to get a pet rock, but I think I might have accidentally bought a very small, very stubborn potato. Now I’m spending my weekends teaching this tuber how to sit, stay, and properly file its own taxes. I even bought it a tiny little business suit and a miniature briefcase so it can network with the neighborhood garden vegetables. My neighbor asked why I was taking a root vegetable to a corporate mixer, so I told him the potato was actually the CEO of a starch-based hedge fund. We’re currently negotiating a merger with a bag of frozen tater tots to create a global potato empire that will eventually overthrow the government.

My dog likes to sleep on the rug. Cats often stare at walls for no reason. Some birds can mimic the sound of a microwave. Hamsters run on wheels while they sleep. Goldfish forget things every few seconds.

I decided to start a strict diet by only eating things that are naturally green. Then I realized that avocado toast counts, so I started adding a side of kale chips for a little extra crunch. To really lean in, I began chewing on the decorative plastic grass in my office lobby just to stay in the zone. Now I'm currently attempting to graze on a freshly manicured golf course while wearing a small cowbell. I’ve finally reached my goal weight, but the local greenskeeper is starting to get really concerned about my grazing habits.

I decided to start a new diet this week. I bought a lot of kale that I will likely throw away. My gym membership costs twenty dollars a month. I really enjoy the taste of almond milk. The scale in my bathroom is very accurate.

I finally retired and decided to spend my golden years mastering the art of professional napping. Now I’m training for the Olympic Sleep-a-thon by practicing power naps in a giant bowl of lukewarm oatmeal. To get in the zone, I’ve hired a tiny choir of squirrels to hum lullabies into my left earlobe. I’ve even started auditing my dreams to ensure the dream-furniture meets strict zoning laws for imaginary suburbs. Last night, I woke up from a nap during a nap just to argue with a holographic toaster about the geopolitical climate of Mars.

Retirement is when you finally have time to organize your socks. You spend most of your Tuesday wondering if the mail has arrived yet. Some people decide to take up bird watching in their backyard. You might find yourself napping in a chair during the middle of the afternoon. It is a period where you no longer have to set an alarm clock for work.

My cell phone provider just offered me a plan with truly unlimited data. It is so unlimited that I can now text people who haven't been born yet. It is so powerful that my phone is currently downloading the actual consciousness of a medieval peasant. I tried to make a call, and I accidentally summoned a small, confused storm cloud into my living room. Now I have to pay an extra five dollars a month to keep the cloud from eating my cat.

My cell phone plan has a very confusing list of monthly fees. The data limits are difficult to track on a small screen. I do not understand why the customer service hold music is so loud. Some plans offer a free subscription to a streaming app. The fine print on the contract is written in a tiny font.

Movie theaters are getting way too expensive for a simple ticket. Now you have to pay twenty dollars for a bucket of popcorn just to enter the building. Then you have to pay a separate fee for the luxury of sitting in a chair that doesn't smell like a gym sock. After that, you're charged a convenience tax for the privilege of not having a stranger breathe directly onto your neck. Finally, they make you pay a subscription fee just to keep the usher from reminding you that you're actually dreaming this entire experience in a cardboard box.

Movie theaters have very expensive popcorn. The seats are usually made of a strange fabric. Some people talk during the film. The screens are incredibly large. There are always a few trailers before the movie starts.

I’m terrified of elevators because I can’t stand the awkward silence. I try to break the ice by asking the strangers if they’ve ever wondered why the buttons are slightly concave. Then I start explaining my theory that the buttons are actually tiny bowls for microscopic soup. This usually leads to me performing a full interpretive dance about a ladle’s journey to the penthouse. By the time the doors open, I’ve usually convinced everyone in the car that I am the rightful King of Floor Four.

Elevators have buttons that light up when you press them. People usually stand in the corners of the car. There is often a small mirror on the back wall. The doors slide open and close automatically. Most elevators play soft music while you ride.

School pickup is basically just a high-stakes game of musical chairs played with two-ton SUVs. You start by politely waiting your turn in the designated lane. Then you realize you’re accidentally blocking a fire hydrant and a small crowd of angry parents has formed a perimeter around your car. Suddenly, you find yourself negotiating a peace treaty with a preschooler who refuses to enter the vehicle unless you promise him a pony and a lifetime supply of gold-plated nuggets. By the time you actually leave, you’ve been declared the provisional mayor of the parking lot and are currently leading a parade of toddlers toward a nearby Taco Bell.

The school pickup line is always full of idling SUVs. Some parents just sit in their cars and stare at the dashboard. The crossing guards wear neon vests that are far too bright. There is always one child who cannot find their backpack. Many of the cones are slightly chipped.

I went to a karaoke bar last night and witnessed a man sing "I Will Survive" so poorly that the room went silent. Then he started singing it again, but this time he replaced all the lyrics with the ingredients of a ham sandwich. He then decided to perform the entire song while slowly descending from the ceiling on a velvet rope. At that point, he began to interpretively dance as a piece of sourdough bread. Finally, he just started screaming the lyrics in a language he invented on the spot while juggling three lukewarm hot dogs.

Karaoke is a hobby where people sing songs they do not know. The microphones are often sticky for no clear reason. Most people choose songs by artists who are no longer alive. The lyrics screen usually scrolls slightly faster than the singer. A lot of people wear outfits they would never wear at a normal job.

I decided to fix the leaky faucet in my bathroom last weekend. Then I realized the pipe was actually a portal to a subterranean kingdom of sentient plumbing fixtures. Now I am currently the Supreme Chancellor of the Copper Pipes and must preside over the Annual Gasket Gala. My first official decree is that all drips must be synchronized to the beat of a funky bass line. Unfortunately, the plumbing nobility is threatening a coup unless I can find a washer that fits a crown made of PVC.

I spent all weekend trying to fix a leaky faucet in my guest bathroom. My toolbox is mostly just a collection of screws I found on the floor. I bought a very expensive flashlight that doesn't actually reach the pipes. The instruction manual for my new water heater is written in a font that is far too small. I think I might just move to a different house instead of replacing the tile.

I finally signed up for a weekly newsletter about artisanal sourdough. Now I get an email every Tuesday telling me how to feed my starter. Then I get an email on Wednesday explaining the spiritual aura of the yeast. By Thursday, the newsletter is demanding that I legally adopt the bread as my primary heir. Now the sourdough is emailing me directly to tell me that my kitchen lighting is insufficient for its nap.

I signed up for a weekly newsletter about gardening. It arrives every Tuesday at ten in the morning. There is a link at the bottom to unsubscribe. The emails often contain photos of tomatoes. I have not checked my inbox in three days.

I went to a car dealership today and the salesman tried to sell me a sedan with a "lifetime warranty." He told me the warranty covers everything from the engine to the tires, and even the air in the cabin. Then he said it also covers any emotional trauma I might experience while driving to work. He then claimed the warranty actually extends to my future children's dental bills. Finally, he insisted the contract guarantees that if I ever get lonely, a professional mime will appear in the passenger seat to keep me company for eternity.

Car dealerships have a lot of balloons parked outside. The salespeople always wear polo shirts with a small logo. There are often large flags waving in the wind. Most of the showrooms have very shiny tile floors. They usually have a small coffee station for the customers.

My new fitness tracker is so aggressive that it sends me a notification if I’ve been sitting still for more than ten minutes. Then it started texting my emergency contacts to let them know I’ve clearly given up on life. Now it's automatically ordering a treadmill and a personal trainer to my house without my permission. It even called my mother to tell her I’m a disappointment who can’t even walk to the mailbox. Finally, it just hacked my bank account and donated all my money to a local marathon because it decided I need a "financial incentive" to move.

Fitness trackers always tell you to stand up when you have been sitting too long. They track how many steps you take to the kitchen. Some of them can monitor your heart rate while you sleep. They send a notification when you have reached your daily goal. Most of them require a charger to keep the battery full.

I love going to farmers markets because you can buy a single organic heirloom tomato for twelve dollars. Then you realize the tomato was hand-massaged by a monk during a full moon. Then you find out the monk was actually a disgraced former tax attorney living in a yurt. Now you're paying an extra five dollars for the tomato's legal representation. Finally, you realize the tomato is actually just a very small, very round piece of driftwood.

Farmers markets are where you pay ten dollars for a single heirloom tomato. The parking lots are always filled with Subarus and woven baskets. Most of the vendors wear linen aprons and wide-brimmed hats. You can find honey that was produced three miles away. There is usually a person selling homemade sourdough bread.

I called my internet provider and was told my estimated wait time was forty-five minutes. After an hour, the automated voice informed me that I had finally reached the fourth circle of hell. Then, a demon answered the phone and asked if I had tried restarting my router in the Lake of Fire. He then put me on hold to consult with Lucifer regarding my data plan. Finally, he transferred me to a representative who was actually just three raccoons in a trench coat eating my credit card.

Customer service hold music is always a low-quality version of a pop song. Most automated menus ask you to say your problem in your own words. Some agents apologize for the delay even though they didn't cause it. Many phone systems disconnect you the moment you get transferred. The hold music eventually loops back to the beginning of the song.

I love long weekends because they give me a few extra days to truly relax. I spent Saturday morning staring at a wall until the wall started asking me for my social security number. By Sunday, I had evolved into a sentient pile of laundry that only communicates through rhythmic belching. On Monday, I accidentally joined a local cult dedicated to the worship of a very specific piece of burnt toast. By Tuesday morning, I had legally changed my name to "Seven" and started a small colony of dust bunnies in my guest bathroom.

Long weekends are a great time to catch up on sleep. Many people decide to take a short trip to a nearby city. Some people spend the extra time cleaning their garages. It is often a time when local parks get a bit more crowded. Most people feel a slight sense of dread on Sunday evening.

I just bought a sunscreen with an SPF of one million. It doesn’t just block the sun, it actually repels the entire concept of light. Now I’m so pale that I’ve started reflecting the hopes and dreams of nearby strangers. If I stand too close to a mirror, I accidentally create a portal to a dimension made of zinc oxide. My skin is now so reflective that NASA is using my left shoulder to calibrate the James Webb Telescope.
Sunscreen is expensive to buy. It feels sticky on the skin. Some brands have a strong smell. It is hard to rub into your back. The bottles often leak in suitcases.

I went to a garage sale today where the prices were so low that the seller actually paid me five dollars to take a rusty toaster. Then he gave me a free bucket of gravel just for mentioning that I liked his shirt. After that, he handed me the deed to his house and asked if I could help him move into a cardboard box. He then insisted that I take his first-born son as a complimentary side dish to the toaster. Finally, he offered to pay my mortgage for the next decade if I would just promise to never tell the police he exists.

Garage sales are mostly just piles of old magazines and chipped mugs. Some people sell a small table for two dollars. Most of the items are just things that didn't fit in the attic. You can find a lot of outdated electronics there. People usually set up the tables on their driveways.

I just started a podcast about the history of silence. It’s a very bold conceptual choice, but the first three episodes are just me staring intensely at a microphone. Now I’ve hired a professional silence coach to help me breathe more quietly during the breaks. I’m currently investing ten thousand dollars into a soundproof bunker to ensure the void is truly authentic. Next week, I’m bringing on a guest who is actually a mime and we’re going to engage in a three-hour conceptual scream-off using only our eyebrows.

Podcasts usually start with a long advertisement for a mattress company. Most hosts have a very specific way of saying the word "fascinating." There are thousands of shows dedicated entirely to true crime. Many people listen to them while they are doing the dishes. Some podcasts are just two friends talking for three hours.

I love going to mattress stores because you get to test out the beds for free. Then you realize you can actually just fall asleep for a few hours while the salesperson watches. Eventually, you decide to just move your toothbrush and a few framed photos into the showroom. Now you're just negotiating a monthly lease with a guy named Gary for a King-size pillow-top. At this point, you’re just paying the store a small fee to let you keep your pajamas on during business hours.

Mattress stores always have a very specific smell. There are usually a lot of people lying down in silence. The sales employees often stand around and wait for you to wake up. Most of the displays have plastic protectors on the corners. Some of them have a few different types of pillows.

I went to the zoo yesterday and saw a gorilla that looked exactly like my uncle. He was wearing my uncle's favorite Hawaiian shirt and holding a miniature cocktail. He then looked me dead in the eye and asked if I had seen his car keys. He proceeded to pull out a tiny set of keys and start trying to unlock the enclosure from the inside. Then he offered me a piece of a banana and asked if I wanted to help him drive to Atlantic City.

The monkeys always look like they are judging your outfit. The gift shop sells plushies that look nothing like the actual animals. The maps are usually printed on paper that rips in the wind. Most of the exhibits just have a sign saying the animal is sleeping. The parking lot is always further away than you expect.

I went bowling last night and managed to knock down all ten pins on my first try. Then I accidentally knocked down the vending machine behind the pins. Then I knocked down the entire building's foundation with one heavy ball. Then I knocked down the concept of gravity itself, sending the whole league floating into the stratosphere. Now I'm currently bowling a strike against a confused nebula in the Andromeda galaxy.

Bowling shoes are the only footwear that look like they were designed for a hospital. The heavy balls make a very specific thumping sound when they hit the lane. Most people spend a lot of time staring at the pins from a distance. The rental counters usually have a small pile of old brochures. The snack bar sells hot dogs that stay warm for a long time.

I love a good potluck because you never know if you're getting gourmet pasta or a bowl of lukewarm grapes. Then there is always that one person who brings a "salad" that is actually just a pile of shredded cabbage and hope. Suddenly, the table is covered in seven different versions of potato salad, including one that tastes like it was seasoned with a battery. Pretty soon, the dinner transforms into a daring game of culinary roulette where the main course is a mysterious casserole that is actively humming. By the end of the night, we are all just staring at a plate of lime-flavored meatballs that have developed their own local government.

Potlucks always feature a bowl of potato salad that has been sitting out too long. Someone always brings a dish that is barely enough for three people. There is usually one person who brings a store-bought platter of crackers. The napkins are always piled in a stack that keeps sliding off the table. Most guests spend ten minutes deciding which mystery casserole to try.

I just used a delivery app that is so efficient they actually predicted I was hungry and sent the food ten minutes before I ordered it. Then they sent a driver to sit in my living room and hand-feed me so I wouldn't have to move my arms. Then the driver started organizing my mail and folding my laundry just to ensure my leisure time was fully optimized. Then he began narrating my life choices in a soothing voice to keep my stress levels low while I ate my tacos. Now he's legally changed his name to my father and is currently paying for my college tuition just to maximize my overall user satisfaction.

Delivery apps have very specific icons for different cuisines. The tracking maps show the driver moving in real time. Most of these apps offer a monthly subscription for free delivery. The estimated arrival time often changes three times before the food arrives. Many people leave a digital tip after the meal is dropped off.

I just flew from New York to Los Angeles and realized that time zones are basically just a giant prank played by the government. It means that while I'm eating dinner here, someone in London is already dreaming about tomorrow's breakfast. Which logically implies that if I fly fast enough, I could actually attend my own birth. Eventually, I'll hit a speed where I arrive at my destination before I've even decided to leave. At that point, I'll be my own grandfather's Uber driver in a dimension where clocks are just circles of sadness.

Time zones make it very confusing to schedule a phone call with someone in Tokyo. The international date line means some people are technically living in tomorrow. Many cities use daylight savings time to adjust for the sun. Most digital clocks update automatically via the internet. Some people find it stressful to keep track of multiple time zones.

I’ve realized that parking lots are the only places where you can spend twenty minutes circling a block just to find a spot that’s actually closer to the entrance than where you started. It’s basically a low-stakes hunger game for people who hate walking. 

I'm not a hiker!

I love the optimism of people who try to squeeze their massive SUV into a "compact only" spot. It’s the only time in a person's life where they look at a clear boundary and think, "I bet if I just angle my mirror, the laws of physics don't apply to me."

Group chats are the only place where you can be completely ignored by twelve people you actually like for three days, and then suddenly be the center of attention because someone sent a slightly controversial opinion about air fryers.

It’s basically a digital hostage situation.

My friends have a group chat that is so active I’ve started treating it like a second job. I don't even read the messages anymore; I just check the notifications to see if I've been fired from the friendship.

I love how hotels have "premium" WiFi that costs twenty dollars a night, but it’s so slow that by the time my email sends, I’ve already checked out. 

I'm basically paying for a digital postcard.
I love staying at hotels because it’s the only place where I can pay three hundred dollars a night to feel like I'm living in a very clean hospital.

I love going to those artisan coffee shops where the menu is just a list of adjectives and the drink costs fifteen dollars. I asked the barista for a medium roast and he looked at me like I’d just asked him to translate an ancient Sumerian tablet.

I just wanted a bean juice, Chad.

I love going to those high-end coffee shops where the menu looks like a chemistry textbook. I just wanted a medium roast, but I accidentally ordered a "deconstructed oat-foam infusion" for twelve dollars.

I’m getting tired of self-checkout machines acting like I’m a high-level criminal just for misplacing a bag of grapes. One wrong move and the machine starts screaming "Unexpected item in bagging area" like it's alerting the SWAT team. 

I’m not a thief, I’m just clumsy!

I love how self-checkout machines act like they’ve never seen a bag of chips before. You scan one item and suddenly the machine has a panic attack and demands a human employee come over to verify that I'm not stealing a family-size bag of Cool Ranch.

Family reunions are the only place where you can be roasted by a cousin you haven't seen in ten years while a great-aunt tells you you've grown so much. It’s basically a hostage situation with potato salad.

I’m still waiting for my ransom.

Family reunions are the only time you can spend six hours with people you share DNA with and still feel like you’re being interrogated by strangers. It’s basically just a high-stakes networking event where the only goal is to find out which cousin is finally in jail.

My cousin just spent forty thousand dollars on a wedding, which is a bold way to start a marriage by immediately agreeing that you both have terrible taste in spreadsheets. 

I'm still waiting for the refund.
I love weddings because it’s the only time you get to see a man spend four thousand dollars on a party just to prove he’s finally stopped making his own decisions.

I spent four hours in gridlock today, and it got so bad that I actually started getting to know the driver in the lane next to me. We’ve reached the stage of our relationship where we’re now discussing our credit scores and potential retirement plans.

We're basically engaged now.
My commute was so slow today that I actually saw a turtle pass me. He didn't even look back; he just gave me a little thumbs-up.

I love how online shopping makes me feel like a high-powered executive until the delivery driver arrives and I realize I just spent eighty dollars on a tiny ergonomic footrest for a cat that doesn't even have a job.

The cat's out of work.

I love the thrill of online shopping, but I’m starting to realize my "treating myself" phase has evolved into a full-blown logistics operation. I’ve reached the point where I’m not even buying things I want anymore; I’m just paying delivery fees to keep the Amazon driver from getting suspicious that I’m not actually home.

I’ve decided to stop buying houseplants because it’s basically just paying twenty dollars to watch a slow-motion crime scene in my living room. I’m not a gardener; I’m a hospice nurse for ferns.

They’re just too dramatic.
I’ve finally given up on trying to keep my houseplants alive. I realized I’m not a "plant parent," I’m just a landlord for a very expensive collection of sticks.

I’m at the age where I’m tired of the "tell me about yourself" question during job interviews, so now I just hand them my therapist's phone number and tell them to call for the full report. 

It’s a real page-turner.
I just had a job interview where the manager asked me where I see myself in five years. I told him "hopefully on the other side of this desk," and he didn't even laugh.

I finally decided to start taking the subway to work, but I quickly realized that "rush hour" is just a polite term for a human Tetris match where nobody wants to be the block.

Still, I love the intimacy of a stranger's shoulder in my ear.

I finally decided to start taking the bus to work to save money on gas. I’ve realized that the commute is actually a great way to practice mindfulness, mostly because I spend forty minutes wondering if the guy sleeping on my shoulder is a passenger or a new roommate.

I finally finished moving into my new place, but I’ve spent the last three days just staring at a mountain of cardboard boxes and wondering which one contains my sanity. I think I packed it in the box labeled "Kitchen Utensils."

Still can't find the whisk.

I finally finished moving into my new apartment, which is great, but I’ve spent the last three days treating my security deposit like a long-distance relationship. I'm just checking in once a week to see if it's actually coming back.

I finally went to the DMV yesterday and the wait was so long that by the time they called my number, my driver's license photo was already out of date. I actually aged three full years in the waiting room.

I'm practically a senior citizen now.

I went to the DMV today and the employee told me my paperwork was incomplete, which is ironic because my patience was already gone. He then asked me to take a seat and wait for my number to be called, which is how I found out that "estimated wait time" is actually just a suggestion from a different dimension.

I’ve realized that video calls are the only time in my life where I can be wearing a dress shirt and pajama pants while staring at my own forehead for forty-five minutes. It's basically a business meeting held in a mirror.

Still a great angle.
I’ve realized the real reason we all hate video calls isn't the technology, it's that for the first time in history, we can actually see the face of the person who is ignoring us in real time.

I’m getting tired of all these streaming services splitting up, because now I have to remember six different passwords just to watch one show. At this rate, I’ll need a separate subscription just to see the credits.

My wallet is exhausted.

I finally decided to cancel my five different streaming subscriptions because I spent four hours last night just scrolling through the menus. I didn’t actually watch any shows, but I did discover that I have a very strong preference for the font they use in the "Recommended" section.

I’ve reached the age where the most stressful part of a birthday party isn't the social anxiety, it's trying to blow out the candles without accidentally coughing a lung into the cake. 

It's a buffet of germs.

I finally reached the age where the "surprise" part of my birthday party is just how many candles it takes to trigger my smoke detector. Now I spend half the cake-cutting ceremony waiting for the fire department to arrive.
